visual_source_files.evidence: Single-page project asset; its denoising, random-avatar, and novel-pose blocks match the Figure 2 narrative at the rendered-asset level, but it is not an editable plot/table generator.
Project-page teaser showing the same geometry/pose visual vocabulary; it supplies no numeric table values or generator source.
Exact project title and author names are present and the page references the teaser/video assets; no figure/table scripts are linked.
Curated Awesome Digital Human list contains the paper title/author entry but is not the author implementation or a visual-source repository.

source_acquisition.search_note: The source inventory row names enhansome/enhansome-digital-human as repository_without_visual_source and lists the exact project page among candidates. GitHub tree/API inspection found no local corpus visual source, no TeX/TikZ/PGF/SVG/notebook, and no plot script or table generator. The exact project page exposes rendered teaser/video assets only. PDF labels, captions, object count, and numeric values remain the sole audit facts; source values are not inferred from the rendered assets.

paper_style.palette_strategy: The paper uses pastel pink/purple/green/orange/blue modules for architecture schematics, saturated normal-like colors for point-cloud and geometry renderings, and muted natural tones for interpolation/body-shape examples. Color carries module, method, rendering-mode, or visual-appearance semantics, but is only partly redundant with labels/layout and is not broadly grayscale-safe.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Captions, text, table rules, arrows, and many labels are vector PDF objects; point clouds, normal maps, UV maps, and project-page imports are raster or mixed. Figure 11 is the only conventional continuous statistical plot; the other figures are architecture diagrams or qualitative montages.
paper_style.style_consistency: The ICLR double-column frame, bold Figure/Table labels, compact booktabs tables, and direct panel labels are consistent across main text and appendix. Figure-internal typography and color rendering vary because imported geometry/PowerPoint-style assets mix with LaTeX text, and small appendix montages are less legible than the main page-width figures.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Geometry distribution.

color.semantic_mapping: Purple blocks/arrows identify the flow stage; multicolored dots and the right-hand human geometry distinguish source samples from the target geometry.

encodings.x: Left-to-right process direction (not a numeric axis)
encodings.color: Source Gaussian points, flow block, and target geometry
encodings.shape: Point cloud versus rounded process block
encodings.text: X ~ N, E(X), and Flow model labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual representation only: no sample size, denominator, repeated runs, scalar metric, or uncertainty is encoded. It depicts Gaussian samples transformed by a flow model into a human geometry distribution.
figures.evidence_relation: Anchors the paper's representation claim and supplies the source-distribution → flow → target-geometry vocabulary reused by Figures 3–4 and the generation results.
design_strengths: A compact directional chain makes the proposed representation legible at a glance.
Direct labels make the latent/source and target roles visible without a separate legend.
design_weaknesses: Single-column scale leaves the point-cloud and output geometry details underspecified.
The caption does not define X, N, E(X), or the meaning of the arrows and therefore is not self-contained.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a three-stage source-distribution / transformation / target-output schematic, but define the random variable and mapping in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.module: Introduction / denoising and two generative tasks

caption.text: Figure 2: (a) Denoising process of a human geometry distribution. (b) Random avatar generation for a given pose. (c) Novel pose generation of a given avatar. Results are rendered from point clouds.

color.semantic_mapping: Normal-like point-cloud colors distinguish geometry views and samples; panel letters and dashed separators carry the task structure.

encodings.x: Denoising/sample progression within each montage row
encodings.color: Rendered point-cloud appearance and pose/identity shading
encodings.facet: Panels (a), (b), and (c) encode denoising, random-avatar, and novel-pose tasks

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative examples only. Panel (a) shows a denoising sequence; panels (b) and (c) show pose-conditioned random avatar generation and avatar-conditioned novel-pose generation. No n, split, error, or uncertainty is reported.
figures.evidence_relation: Turns Figure 1's distribution primitive into the two generation tasks later evaluated qualitatively in Figures 8–9 and appendix Figures 12–14; Table 4 carries the separate FID comparison.
design_strengths: Combines process, task branching, and rendered output in one high-level entry point.
Panel letters and layout make the three task roles easy to scan.
design_weaknesses: The denoising step count and the identity/pose conditioning inputs are not recoverable from the panel.
Many small human renderings lose geometric detail at page scale, and the caption does not explain the color/shading semantics.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a denoising progression with task-specific qualitative branches; state the conditioning variables and sampling rule alongside the panel labels.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Aggregated samples (x′0 , x1 ).

color.semantic_mapping: Colored point clouds show the SMPL/template and human-geometry samples; arrows and the aggregation block encode pair construction.

encodings.line: Directional arrows into an aggregate pair

figures.data_and_statistics: Diagrammatic training-pair construction; x′0 and x1 are shown as paired samples rather than plotted observations. No quantitative statistic or uncertainty is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Explains the aggregation choice used before the conditional generation network in Figure 4 and motivates the pair-construction ablation in Figure 6.
design_strengths: The paired-sample idea is reduced to a simple visual operation.
Mathematical sample labels connect the diagram directly to the method notation.
design_weaknesses: Caption-only title leaves the aggregation operation and the roles of x′0/x1 unexplained.
Small single-column rendering makes point-level correspondence difficult to inspect.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show training-pair formation as a labeled source/target flow, with one sentence defining each sample and the aggregation operator.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Overview of our method. (a) We encode a geometry into a feature map, which is decompressed with a SMPL vertex map. The decompressed feature serves as a condition for our denoising network. (b) The human generation task is formulated as the conditional generation of feature maps, guided by the SMPL vertex map, optionally incorporating additional conditioning inputs.

color.semantic_mapping: Pastel colored blocks distinguish geometry/feature representations, decompression, SMPL conditioning, and denoising; arrows encode data flow.

encodings.shape: Rounded boxes for operations, geometry icons for inputs/outputs
encodings.text: Module names, SMPL vertex map, and conditioning labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Architecture overview; it encodes no empirical measurements. The two panels specify the feature-map condition, SMPL vertex-map guidance, optional conditioning inputs, and denoising-network path.
figures.evidence_relation: Provides the method contract linking Figure 3's pair construction to the output distribution and later controls in Figures 9, 12, 17, and 21.
design_strengths: Panel split separates representation encoding from conditional generation while retaining a shared visual grammar.
Direct module labels and directional arrows expose the computational dependency graph.
design_weaknesses: Several connector labels and small boxes compete for space at page width.
The caption names the pathway but does not define tensor shapes, conditioning precedence, or which blocks are learned versus fixed.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use paired encoding/generation panels with a common representation color and explicit arrows; include tensor roles and optional-control semantics in a companion legend or caption.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Single-geometry fitting visualization.

color.semantic_mapping: Colored geometry renderings distinguish the target and fitted/reconstructed single geometry; labels and panel arrangement provide the comparison key.

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative single-geometry fitting visualization used in the ablation. It reports no fitted distance, sample count, optimization trajectory, or uncertainty; the numerical surface-distance comparison is Table 3.
figures.evidence_relation: Supplies visual evidence for the single-geometry fitting design in Section 5.1.2 and complements the surface-distance values in Table 3.
design_strengths: A direct rendered comparison makes the ablation motivation concrete.
Single-column placement keeps the visual adjacent to the fitting discussion.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not identify the columns, target/reference status, or fitting protocol.
Without a metric or scale, visual similarity cannot establish the quantitative claim by itself.
figures.reusable_pattern: Place target/fitted geometry side by side and pair the montage with an explicit metric definition and fitting protocol.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Comparison of strategies for constructing training pairs. The first row shows our proposed strategy, the second row finds the nearest points on the SMPL mesh.

color.semantic_mapping: Rows encode pair-construction strategies and point/mesh geometry is shown with normal-like colors; row labels are the primary redundant encoding.

encodings.y: Rows encode proposed versus nearest-SMPL strategy

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative ablation over pair-construction strategies. It contains no aggregate error, n, or uncertainty; the visual purpose is to expose correspondence quality and motivate the subsequent surface-distance test.
figures.evidence_relation: Connects the training-pair design decision to Table 3's surface-distance comparison and to Figure 3's aggregate-pair mechanism.
design_strengths: Two rows make the design comparison immediately inspectable.
The examples expose a correspondence mechanism rather than only a final score.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not specify the number or selection rule of cases.
Color and small geometry details are not reliably distinguishable in grayscale or at single-column width.
figures.reusable_pattern: Compare correspondence strategies in aligned rows, with a row-level definition and a paired quantitative distance table.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Visualization results of different geometry distribution formulations at the 30, 000th training iteration. GT represents the ground-truth result.

color.semantic_mapping: Method columns use rendered point/normal colors; direct method labels and GT identify the comparison categories.

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative comparison at the stated 30,000th training iteration. It does not encode the Chamfer scalar values or uncertainty; Table 2 and Figure 11 provide the numerical/trajectory evidence for these formulations.
figures.evidence_relation: Links the formulation ablation to the iteration-controlled visual comparison and to Table 2's single/dataset Chamfer values.
design_strengths: A common iteration checkpoint makes the visual comparison temporally interpretable.
GT and method labels provide a direct reading path without a remote legend.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not enumerate the formulations or explain which row/column is being compared.
A single checkpoint can hide convergence differences and is not a substitute for the trajectory in Figure 11.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a fixed-checkpoint aligned grid for formulation comparisons, backed by a scalar table and convergence curve.

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8: Qualitative comparisons of human generation results. Existing methods are displayed with both rendering results and raw geometry outputs, typically organized as two columns each. We include two geometry samples generated by our method for comparison.

color.semantic_mapping: Rows/columns encode method and rendering mode; normal-like and point-cloud colors preserve geometry cues, while direct labels identify method blocks.

encodings.x: Columns group raw geometry and enhanced rendering
encodings.shape: Rendered human silhouettes and raw point geometry

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative multi-method comparison; no sample denominator, selection rule, or uncertainty is encoded. Table 4 supplies FID for raw and enhanced rendering, while this figure exposes visual artifacts and geometry quality.
figures.evidence_relation: Main qualitative counterpart to Table 4: it grounds the raw/enhanced rendering distinction and shows the geometries behind the FID comparison.
design_strengths: Page-width layout supports aligned method-by-rendering comparisons.
Showing raw geometry alongside renderings makes the evaluation target more transparent than rendered images alone.
design_weaknesses: Many methods and columns create a dense scan path and small individual examples.
The caption does not name the methods, define sample selection, or state whether all methods use the same poses.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair each method's raw representation with its rendered output in aligned columns and bind the grid to the same rows and sample protocol as the metric table.

figures.label: Figure 9

caption.text: Figure 9: Generating different poses for a given avatar. We showcase challenging cases, including exaggerated poses, skirts, and loose outfits.

color.semantic_mapping: Consistent avatar colors/appearance across pose columns encode identity preservation; pose silhouettes and direct layout encode the conditioning change.

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative novel-pose generation for fixed avatars, emphasizing exaggerated poses, skirts, and loose outfits. No pose count, subject denominator, failure rate, or uncertainty is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Extends Figure 2(c) from overview to challenging cases and complements the fixed-feature and novel-pose evidence in appendix Figures 12–16.
design_strengths: Fixed-avatar rows make identity preservation and deformation behavior visually salient.
Challenging cases target the stated geometry-distribution advantage rather than only easy poses.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not define the pose set or explain how avatar identity is held fixed.
Qualitative examples cannot establish coverage of the pose/clothing distribution or failure frequency.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use aligned fixed-identity pose rows and explicitly report the pose set, subject count, and any omitted failures.

figures.label: Figure 10

caption.text: Figure 10: Details of our auto-decoder. (a) We sample noise from a Gaussian distribution (R3 ) and generate the flow that transforms from the SMPL template distribution to the human geometry distribution. (b) A convolutional network is used to interpret and decompress the compact feature map with the SMPL vertex map. (c) The architecture details of our model.

color.semantic_mapping: Pastel module fills identify Gaussian/flow, feature-map decompression, SMPL conditioning, and network blocks; arrows encode the decoder pathway.

encodings.text: Module names, R3, SMPL vertex map, and layer labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Architecture details only; no measured activation, parameter count, sample size, or uncertainty. Panel (a) gives the distribution transform, panel (b) the decompression path, and panel (c) the detailed network layout.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix expansion of Figure 4: makes the auto-decoder and SMPL-conditioned decompression pathway more reproducible and connects the conceptual method to implementation detail.
design_strengths: Three panels progressively move from probabilistic transform to decoder pathway to layer-level detail.
The appendix placement preserves main-text flow while exposing implementation structure for reproduction.
design_weaknesses: Dense labels and mixed typography make panel (c) difficult to parse without the surrounding text.
The caption still omits tensor dimensions, layer widths, and exact activation/normalization choices.
figures.reusable_pattern: Provide a progressive architecture appendix: distribution-level overview, tensor pathway, and layer-level diagram, with dimensions in an accompanying table.

figures.label: Figure 11

caption.text: Figure 11: The evolution of the Chamfer distance of training different distribution formulations.

color.semantic_mapping: Each colored line identifies a geometry-distribution formulation; line color is the primary series encoding and the legend is required to decode it.

figures.data_and_statistics: Single training trajectory plot with three formulation curves over iteration; the visible y-axis is logarithmic and no replicate traces, error bars, confidence bands, or run-level uncertainty are shown. Table 2 reports selected endpoint values.
figures.evidence_relation: Provides trajectory evidence for the formulation choice behind Table 2 and Figure 7, but remains a single-run convergence trace rather than a population summary.
design_strengths: Log y-scale exposes early convergence differences across formulations.
A compact legend and common axes support direct trajectory comparison.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not identify the curve names or training-run count, and the single-column legend is small.
No variability across seeds or data splits is shown, so curve separation should not be read as uncertainty-aware evidence.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a common log-scale convergence chart for ablations and pair endpoint values with an explicit multi-run variability statement.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.module: Appendix 9.3 / fixed geometry feature across poses

caption.text: Figure 12: Demonstrations of different methods with fixed geometry features across varying poses. All results show identical geometric details in different poses.

color.semantic_mapping: Method colors/labels distinguish rows while repeated geometry details across pose columns encode feature preservation.

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative fixed-feature pose sweep. It asserts identical geometric details across poses but gives no pointwise correspondence metric, number of identities/poses, or uncertainty; the claim is visual and bounded to shown examples.
figures.evidence_relation: Directly tests the conditional-control promise from Figure 4 and extends Figure 9 with cross-method fixed-feature evidence.
design_strengths: Aligned pose columns make preservation of clothing and fine details easy to inspect.
The caption states the intended invariant rather than leaving the reader to infer it.
design_weaknesses: The methods are not named in the caption and the visual “identical” claim lacks a quantitative correspondence measure.
Dense repeated panels and low-saturation details reduce readability at appendix scale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Hold a geometry feature fixed and sweep pose in aligned columns, while reporting an explicit geometry-consistency metric beside the qualitative grid.

figures.label: Figure 13

caption.text: Figure 13: Novel pose generation results.

color.semantic_mapping: Rendered geometry colors and pose silhouettes encode qualitative generation outputs; row/column alignment supplies the comparison structure.

figures.data_and_statistics: Additional qualitative novel-pose samples; no denominator, pose sampling protocol, or failure accounting is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Adds appendix breadth to the novel-pose claim introduced in Figures 2 and 9, without changing the paper's quantitative evidence boundary.
design_strengths: More examples test the method beyond the main-text showcase.
Aligned grids allow identity and pose changes to be visually separated.
design_weaknesses: Caption-only labeling gives no selection or coverage information.
The appendix montage may encourage anecdotal generalization because omissions and failures are not visible.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use an appendix gallery for breadth, but pair it with a declared sampling frame and an accounting of included/omitted cases.

figures.label: Figure 14

caption.text: Figure 14: This figure shows the results of our method after full training, using the same identities and poses as in Fig. 7.

color.semantic_mapping: Repeated identity/pose appearance and direct grid alignment encode the matched comparison to Figure 7.

encodings.y: Rows show output/reference or formulation cases

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative matched-case follow-up after full training. It has no new scalar statistic or uncertainty; its evidentiary value is the controlled reuse of the identities and poses from Figure 7.
figures.evidence_relation: Closes the fixed-iteration versus full-training comparison and makes the appendix-to-main linkage explicit through the Fig. 7 pointer.
design_strengths: Reusing the same cases improves within-paper comparability.
The caption states the control condition and training status.
design_weaknesses: The small figure does not show the full original grid, making exact matching laborious.
No training duration/iteration count or visual-difference criterion is supplied.
figures.reusable_pattern: Reuse a named main-text subset after full training, with identical ordering and an explicit side-by-side difference cue.

figures.label: Figure 15

caption.text: Figure 15: This figure shows challenging examples with loose clothing and hair. Our point-based representation may exhibit small local sparsity in extreme cases, but nevertheless, we maintain high geometric quality overall. To demonstrate this, we apply Poisson surface reconstruction to our results, shown on the right.

color.semantic_mapping: Rendered point geometry and Poisson surfaces distinguish raw point-based outputs from reconstructed surfaces; paired layout is redundant with the right-side reconstruction.

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative stress cases for loose clothing and hair. The caption acknowledges local sparsity and shows Poisson reconstruction as a visualization; it provides no sparsity rate, failure denominator, reconstruction parameters, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: This is the clearest failure-boundary evidence for the point representation and links the claimed high geometry quality to a visible raw-versus-reconstructed check.
design_strengths: Explicitly surfaces an edge case instead of presenting only ideal outputs.
Paired raw and reconstructed views help distinguish sampling sparsity from surface quality.
design_weaknesses: “High geometric quality overall” is not quantified and the displayed cases can be selected.
Poisson reconstruction introduces a second processing step whose parameters and effect are not documented in the caption.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show stress cases with the raw representation next to a reconstruction, and report the case frame, reconstruction settings, and failure frequency.

figures.label: Figure 16

caption.text: Figure 16: This figure illustrates large deformations of loose clothing under extreme poses.

color.semantic_mapping: Clothing silhouette and rendered geometry encode deformation under pose change; aligned pairs provide the main redundant cue.

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative extreme-pose deformation examples. No pose-angle range, garment count, failure rate, or quantitative deformation error is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Narrows the general novel-pose claim to an explicit loose-clothing stress case and complements Figure 15's sparsity discussion.
design_strengths: Extreme poses target a known difficult mode and make deformation behavior visible.
Paired examples support a direct before/after reading.
design_weaknesses: The caption does not define “large” or the pose-selection threshold.
The examples lack an accompanying deformation metric or coverage denominator.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use paired extreme-pose clothing examples with a defined pose severity measure and a quantitative deformation-consistency companion.

figures.label: Figure 17

caption.text: Figure 17: Given the same feature map, the figure shows the generated results for different SMPL body shapes and genders. Since the underlying identity feature map remains unchanged, the gender differences mainly appear as subtle variations in body shape.

color.semantic_mapping: Rows/columns encode SMPL shape/gender conditions while the repeated feature-map identity is represented by shared clothing/geometry cues.

encodings.x: Columns vary SMPL body shape/gender condition

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative conditional-control demonstration with the same feature map and varied SMPL body shape/gender. It reports no number of conditions, body-shape parameter values, or quantitative identity-preservation error.
figures.evidence_relation: Tests the optional SMPL conditioning described in Figure 4 and shows that the identity feature map is intended to remain fixed while body condition changes.
design_strengths: The controlled same-feature-map setup isolates the conditioning intervention.
The caption states the expected subtlety of gender differences and avoids claiming a new identity.
design_weaknesses: Subtle variations are difficult to verify in low-saturation thumbnails.
Exact SMPL parameters and the criterion for “unchanged” identity are not supplied.
figures.reusable_pattern: Hold the identity feature fixed and sweep an explicit body-condition grid, reporting parameter values and an identity-invariance measure.

figures.label: Figure 18

caption.text: Figure 18: The figure shows interpolation results between the leftmost and rightmost identities; note how new clothing wrinkles, styles, and hairstyles naturally emerge during the transition.

color.semantic_mapping: Continuous visual changes in clothing, wrinkles, style, and hair encode interpolation along the identity-feature path.

encodings.x: Interpolation position from left to right identity

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative identity interpolation between endpoint identities. The interpolation schedule, number of intermediate points, latent-space distance, and failure/uncertainty are not encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Provides appendix evidence for smooth geometry-distribution support and the emergence of nontrivial clothing/hair details between identities.
design_strengths: Endpoint-to-endpoint layout gives a clear reading direction.
The caption identifies the intended emergent attributes rather than only showing images.
design_weaknesses: “Naturally emerge” is an interpretation without a defined smoothness or novelty metric.
Only a small number of identity pairs are shown and the interpolation parameterization is unspecified.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show endpoint-conditioned interpolation strips with an explicit parameter schedule and a measurable smoothness/novelty diagnostic.

figures.label: Figure 19

caption.text: Figure 19: Interpolations. This figure presents interpolations between identities wearing outerwear.

color.semantic_mapping: Outerwear silhouette and texture vary along endpoint-to-endpoint interpolation; consistent row ordering supplies the comparison structure.

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative interpolation strips for identities wearing outerwear. No schedule, pair count, or quantitative continuity/identity metric is encoded.
figures.evidence_relation: Extends Figure 18 to a clothing-specific appendix case and supports the claim that the distribution can express outerwear variation.
design_strengths: Outerwear makes intermediate clothing changes visible.
Page-width placement accommodates a sequence of multiple identity states.
design_weaknesses: The one-word “Interpolations” lead-in is redundant and the caption lacks the interpolation method.
Anecdotal strips do not establish coverage across outerwear styles or identity pairs.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a clothing-focused interpolation strip with endpoint metadata, interpolation weights, and a continuity check.

figures.label: Figure 20

caption.text: Figure 20: UV parameterization of the SMPL template.

color.semantic_mapping: High-saturation UV regions encode template parameterization patches; patch boundaries and layout provide geometric redundancy.

figures.data_and_statistics: Template parameterization map; no empirical statistic, sample count, or uncertainty. The color regions describe the UV assignment used to align SMPL vertices/features, not a scalar performance field.
figures.evidence_relation: Supports Figure 4 and Figure 10 by making the SMPL vertex-map/UV alignment concrete and gives a reproduction-oriented view of the template coordinate system.
design_strengths: Colorful surface map exposes the spatial correspondence structure compactly.
The appendix location keeps an implementation prerequisite available without interrupting the main result narrative.
design_weaknesses: Caption does not define U/V ranges, patch indexing, seam convention, or whether colors are categorical.
Highly saturated colors are not grayscale-safe and can obscure fine topology at single-column width.
figures.reusable_pattern: Document template parameterization with labeled U/V axes, seam convention, patch indices, and a colorblind-safe redundant boundary encoding.

figures.label: Figure 21

caption.text: Figure 21: Given our high-quality geometries, textures can be synthesized in various ways. Here, we first generate multi-view images with a depth-conditioned video generation model (Wan2.1), and then optimize point colors via Gaussian Splatting.

color.semantic_mapping: Rendered texture/geometry appearance distinguishes multi-view synthesis from optimized point colors; arrows and method labels encode the pipeline.

encodings.facet: Input geometry → multi-view video → Gaussian Splatting output

figures.data_and_statistics: Qualitative texture-synthesis pipeline and outputs. It specifies Wan2.1 depth-conditioned multi-view image generation followed by Gaussian Splatting point-color optimization, but gives no image count, optimization settings, or texture metric.
figures.evidence_relation: Extends the geometry representation into a downstream texturing use case and makes the dependency on high-quality geometry explicit.
design_strengths: Pipeline arrows connect the generated geometry to a concrete downstream rendering procedure.
The caption names the external video model and Gaussian Splatting stage, improving reproducibility relative to an unlabeled gallery.
design_weaknesses: The visual result does not isolate geometry quality from texture/video-model quality.
No protocol, input-view count, color-loss, or artifact accounting is given, so the panel cannot validate the downstream method quantitatively.
figures.reusable_pattern: Show downstream synthesis as an explicit stage graph with input/output examples and report the external model version and optimization protocol.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Comparison of 3D human representation methods.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty; categorical capability checks only.
tables.data_and_statistics: Seven method rows (Tri-plane + NeRF, Template-based, Primitive Volumes, Mesh-based, Point-based, Implicit Function, and Geometry Distributions (Ours)) are marked for Loose Clothing, Scalability, and Fine Details. The Ours row is the only row checked in all three columns.
tables.evidence_relation: Defines the representation trade-off that motivates the geometry-distribution design and foreshadows the loose-clothing/fine-detail qualitative evidence in Figures 8, 9, and 15–17.
design_strengths: A compact capability matrix exposes the paper's design target without numerical overclaiming.
Three binary columns make the intended trade-off easy to compare across methods.
design_weaknesses: Capability checks are asserted without operational definitions or supporting measurements.
Cell shading/bold emphasis can be ambiguous in grayscale and there is no citation or evidence note per method.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a capability matrix for representation choices, but define each capability and link it to an empirical test or citation.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2: Chamfer distance of different distribution formulations.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty or replicate summary; entries are single Chamfer values at the stated checkpoints.
tables.data_and_statistics: Columns are Zhang et al., w/o Pairs, w/o DistNorm, and Ours; rows are Single and Dataset. Values are Single: 0.0083, 0.0040, 0.0020, 0.0032; Dataset: 0.0101, 0.0706, 0.0071, 0.0032. Single is lowest for w/o DistNorm, while Dataset is lowest for Ours. Single uses 10,000 iterations and Dataset uses 30,000 iterations.
tables.evidence_relation: Quantifies the formulation ablation shown qualitatively in Figure 7 and traces its training dynamics in Figure 11; the row-specific iteration checkpoints bound the comparison.
design_strengths: Four-decimal precision preserves small Chamfer differences.
The Single/Dataset row split makes the generalization of the formulation choice visible.
design_weaknesses: Point estimates omit seeds, variance, and the number of geometries behind each value.
The caption does not state the iteration checkpoints or define why the baseline is named Zhang et al.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair a small ablation table with a matched visual grid and convergence curve, while reporting checkpoint and replicate metadata.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3: Surface distance comparison between various designs.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty or replicate summary; values are point estimates of Surface Distance (lower is better).
tables.data_and_statistics: Rows are VecSet, FeatureMap, and Ours with Surface Distance values 0.0018, 0.0014, and 0.0012 respectively; the column header includes a downward arrow.
tables.evidence_relation: Provides the quantitative counterpart to the single-geometry fitting visualization in Figure 5 and the pair-construction comparison in Figure 6.
design_strengths: Single metric column and downward-arrow header make the direction of improvement explicit.
Four decimals distinguish the closely spaced design variants.
design_weaknesses: Surface Distance is not defined in the caption and no evaluation population or fitting protocol is shown.
No variance or paired-case information accompanies the small differences.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a one-metric design ablation table with an explicit metric definition, evaluation unit, and uncertainty/paired-difference note.

tables.label: Table 4
tables.module: Results 5.3 / FID raw and enhanced rendering

caption.text: Table 4: Comparison of FID scores. The * results are adopted from E3Gen (Zhang et al., 2024d). For some methods, the results are rendered directly from their raw geometries, so the numbers in both rows are identical.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty or replicate summary; FID values are point estimates for the two rendering rows.
tables.data_and_statistics: Columns are ENARF*, GNARF*, EVA3D*, E3Gen, GetAvatar, gDNA, and Ours; Raw Geometry values are 223.72, 166.62, 60.37, 65.32, 56.07, 42.90, 16.16; Enhanced Rendering values are 223.72, 166.62, 60.37, 28.12, 22.77, 17.43, 16.16. The caption marks adopted values with * and explains identical raw/enhanced entries for methods rendered directly from raw geometry.
tables.evidence_relation: Quantifies the raw-versus-enhanced rendering comparison shown in Figure 8. The manuscript text defines FID here as comparison between rendered normal images and GT normal maps, using 50 views per subject and 25,000 normal images.
design_strengths: Two explicit rendering rows expose whether postprocessing changes the metric.
The * marker and caption preserve provenance for adopted baseline results.
design_weaknesses: No uncertainty, subject-level distribution, or confidence information is reported for large FID differences.
The wide seven-method header is dense and the caption does not repeat the normal-map evaluation protocol.
tables.reusable_pattern: Separate representation/rendering conditions into rows, retain provenance markers, and place the image comparison next to the same metric definition.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5: User study on quality and physical plausibility.

tables.uncertainty: No uncertainty, agreement, or participant-level spread; entries are mean ratings on a 1–5 scale.
tables.data_and_statistics: Columns are Metric, GetAvatar, gDNA, E3Gen, and Ours. Quality means are 2.16, 2.54, 2.12, and 4.04; Plausibility means are 2.20, 2.66, 2.08, and 4.36. The study uses 2 identities × 8 poses, 25 participants, and a 1–5 rating scale.
tables.evidence_relation: Supplies the human-evaluation counterpart to the generated examples in Figures 8–9 and supports the quality/physical-plausibility claims in Results 5.4.
design_strengths: Metric rows and a fixed rating scale make the user-study comparison compact.
Method columns align directly with the qualitative comparison methods.
design_weaknesses: Means alone hide participant agreement, variance, and question wording.
The caption does not state the sample/participant protocol or whether raters saw randomized paired comparisons.
tables.reusable_pattern: Report human-rating means beside sample counts, scale anchors, and participant-level uncertainty/agreement measures.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: The visual narrative moves from the distribution concept (Figures 1–2), to pair construction and conditional decoding (Figures 3–4), to fitting/formulation ablations (Figures 5–7 and Tables 2–3), to raw/enhanced generation and novel-pose results (Figures 8–9 and Tables 4–5), then expands in the appendix into decoder details, convergence, conditioning, stress cases, interpolation, UV alignment, and texturing (Figures 10–21).
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions consistently bold the Figure label and usually provide a title plus a short setup or panel key. Main result captions identify rendering/task structure more often than they state findings; appendix captions sometimes state a qualitative finding or limitation (Figures 15–18). Captions rarely provide sample denominators, protocols, or uncertainty.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Tables use compact one-level headers, booktabs-like horizontal rules, bold best/selected entries, and occasional cell shading/check marks. Headers generally encode method columns and a metric direction arrow, but metric definitions, evaluation units, and uncertainty are kept in nearby prose rather than the table itself.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figures 3–4 define the aggregation, feature-map, SMPL-map, and denoising mechanism; Figures 5–7 and Tables 2–3 test pair construction, fitting design, and distribution formulations; Figures 8–9 and Tables 4–5 connect the selected design to generation quality, rendering, pose control, and human ratings. Figure 11 supplies the only explicit trajectory link.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: Appendix Figures 10–21 are deliberate expansions rather than a second visual language: Figure 10 details Figure 4, Figure 11 extends Table 2/Figure 7, Figures 12–17 expand Figures 2/9 and the conditional-control/failure claims, Figures 18–20 document interpolation and UV infrastructure, and Figure 21 shows a downstream texturing use case.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: LaTeX body/caption/table text is broadly Times/Nimbus Roman and Computer Modern math, but imported diagrams and geometry assets introduce Cambria, Aptos, SegoePrint, BrushScriptMT, and varying small labels. Main page-width objects are readable; single-column figures and appendix labels frequently approach 6–7 pt.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Purple/pastel modules recur in conceptual/architecture diagrams, saturated normal-like colors recur in geometry renderings, and muted earth tones recur for identity interpolation and body-condition examples. These palettes are semantically coherent within object families but not globally colorblind/grayscale safe, and no shared quantitative color scale exists.

most_reusable_patterns: Use an overview montage that combines a process sequence with clearly labeled task branches.
Align raw representations with rendered outputs so metric rows and visual artifacts refer to the same object.
Pair controlled qualitative grids with a scalar ablation table and a convergence trajectory.
Expose stress cases with raw-versus-reconstructed views and state the limitation in the caption.
failure_patterns: Captions often name a visual object without defining sample selection, denominators, metrics, or conditioning protocol.
Most qualitative panels and all reported tables lack uncertainty, replicate information, or failure accounting.
Small imported montages and saturated colors reduce grayscale and appendix readability.
Capability checks and claims such as “identical” or “high geometric quality” are not accompanied by operational definitions or quantitative bounds.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper uses a coherent distribution-to-geometry story built from compact architecture schematics, aligned qualitative renderings, and sparse point-estimate tables, with strong mechanism/result linkage but limited protocol, uncertainty, and accessibility detail.
